An amanuensis is a person whose job is to write down exactly what another person says, or to copy out a piece of writing by hand on someone else's behalf. Think of them as a human pen — their hand does the physical writing, but the words, thoughts, and ideas all belong to someone else. They contribute no content of their own. They are purely a recorder.

The plural form is amanuenses.
What Does an Amanuensis Actually Do?

The role has two closely related functions:

1. Taking dictation. The amanuensis listens as someone speaks and writes down every word, exactly as spoken. The speaker is the thinker and creator; the amanuensis is the instrument. If the speaker says "write this letter to my brother," the amanuensis picks up a quill (or pen) and writes it, word for word.

2. Copying documents by hand. Before printing presses were widespread, important texts — books, legal papers, scriptures, manuscripts — had to be duplicated by hand. An amanuensis would sit and copy out an existing text, letter by letter, producing a faithful replica. Again, they are not creating anything — they are reproducing.

To understand why this word matters, you have to picture the world before typewriters, computers, voice recorders, and photocopiers. If a scholar wanted ten copies of a manuscript, someone had to sit down and write it out ten times by hand. If a great thinker was old, unwell, or — crucially — blind, they could not physically write their own thoughts. They needed a trusted person to sit beside them and write on their behalf.

This was an extremely common and important role throughout history. Some of the most celebrated figures in literature, music, and philosophy depended on amanuenses to get their work into the world:

  • The poet John Milton, after going completely blind, dictated his epic poem Paradise Lost to his daughters and others who served as his amanuenses. The words were entirely his; the hand was theirs.
  • Beethoven, as his hearing deteriorated, used amanuenses to help manage correspondence.
  • Ancient Roman scholars and statesmen, including Cicero, kept trained slaves or assistants specifically to write at their dictation.

In legal and religious institutions, teams of amanuenses were employed to copy laws, contracts, holy texts, and official records — preserving knowledge and enabling it to be shared across distances.

The single most important thing to understand about an amanuensis is what they are not doing: they are not contributing any ideas, judgment, or creativity. This is what makes the word precise and distinct.

Compare them with:

  • A ghostwriter, who secretly creates the content that appears under someone else's name. A ghostwriter is the actual author, working invisibly. An amanuensis is not the author at all — they are simply the writing instrument.
  • An editor, who reads someone's work and improves, corrects, or reshapes it. An amanuensis does none of that — they record faithfully and exactly, without alteration.
  • A translator, who converts meaning from one language to another. An amanuensis stays entirely within the original language and the original words.

An amanuensis is defined by total fidelity and total self-effacement. Their personal voice is irrelevant. Their opinion is irrelevant. They exist in that moment purely to serve the act of inscription.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Amanuensis" is a formal, literary word. You will encounter it most often in historical writing, biography, academic texts, and literary criticism. In everyday modern speech, people tend to say "secretary," "personal assistant," or "transcriptionist" instead.

However, "amanuensis" carries a slightly richer and more specific meaning than any of those modern substitutes. It implies a closer, more personal, and often more intellectual relationship — a dedicated human recorder who works intimately with a thinker or creator, not just an office worker handling administrative tasks.

You might also see it used figuratively, where a writer or artist describes technology — or even their own hand — as their "amanuensis," meaning the passive instrument through which their ideas take physical form.

• "After the philosopher lost the use of his hands, he hired an amanuensis who would sit with him each morning and transcribe his thoughts."
  • "The monks worked as amanuenses for centuries, copying sacred texts so that the knowledge would not be lost."
  • "She was more than a secretary — she became his trusted amanuensis, accompanying him everywhere and writing down every word he wished to preserve."
  • "The manuscript, though written in a different hand, was confirmed to be the author's work; scholars established that she had used an amanuensis during her final illness."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: an amanuensis is a person who writes down another person's words or copies their texts, contributing no ideas of their own — a human instrument of transcription.
